new.title: Climb to Notre-Dame de la Garde for the best view
new.desc: The neo-Byzantine basilica by Henri-Jacques Espérandieu was begun in 1853 and consecrated in 1864 on a limestone hill above the city. A gilded Virgin and Child about 11 m tall crowns the bell tower. Known as la Bonne Mère, it gives 360-degree views of the city and harbour.
new.tip: Free entry, open daily roughly 7:00 to 18:00 (check seasonal hours); go at sunset, or take bus 60 from the Vieux-Port.
new.q: Basilique Notre-Dame de la Garde, Rue Fort du Sanctuaire, Marseille

new.title: Admire yourself in the Vieux-Port mirror canopy
new.desc: The Ombrière, a polished-steel canopy about 48 m by 22 m on eight posts, was designed by Foster + Partners with landscape architect Michel Desvigne and installed in 2013, when Marseille was European Capital of Culture. It mirrors passers-by, boats and sky on the old harbour, where Greeks founded Massalia around 600 BC.
new.tip: Free. Stand beneath it for photos; the quay is liveliest in the morning.
new.q: Ombrière du Vieux-Port, Quai des Belges, Marseille

new.title: Explore the MuCEM and cross to Fort Saint-Jean
new.desc: The Museum of European and Mediterranean Civilisations, opened in 2013 in Rudy Ricciotti's lattice-clad cube, links by footbridge to the 17th-century Fort Saint-Jean. The fort's terraces and gardens have sea views.
new.tip: Closed on Tuesdays (except in August) and on 1 May and 25 December. The fort grounds are free; exhibitions are ticketed.
new.q: MuCEM, 7 Promenade Robert Laffont, Marseille

new.title: See the cantilevered Villa Méditerranée
new.desc: Stefano Boeri's building, finished for Marseille-Provence 2013, has a dramatic cantilever hanging over a reflecting pool on the J4 esplanade beside the MuCEM. It is an international centre for Mediterranean dialogue and exhibitions, and its basement holds the Cosquer Méditerranée cave replica.
new.tip: The pool and esplanade can be seen free from outside. Check villa-mediterranee.org for exhibitions.
new.q: Villa Méditerranée, Esplanade du J4, Marseille

new.title: Visit the striped Cathédrale de la Major
new.desc: One of the largest cathedrals built in 19th-century Europe (1852-1893), in Roman-Byzantine style with white and green striped stone. It stands beside the remains of the older Romanesque Vieille Major.
new.tip: Free entry, typically from 10:00; hours and the weekly closing day vary by source, so check before going. Walk over from the MuCEM.
new.q: Cathédrale de la Major, Place de la Major, Marseille

new.title: Wander the Vieille Charité courtyard
new.desc: Pierre Puget designed this 17th-century almshouse around an arcaded courtyard with a baroque chapel. It now hosts the Museum of Mediterranean Archaeology and the Museum of African, Oceanic and Amerindian Arts, plus the poetry centre cipM.
new.tip: The courtyard is free; museums are ticketed and closed on Mondays (except Easter and Whit Monday).
new.q: Centre de la Vieille Charité, 2 Rue de la Charité, Marseille

new.title: Descend into the crypts of Abbaye Saint-Victor
new.desc: A fortified abbey whose origins go back to the 5th century (tradition credits John Cassian), with early Christian crypts and sarcophagi. The present church dates mostly from the 11th century.
new.tip: Basilica open roughly 9:00 to 19:00; the crypts have a small entry fee (about 2 euros). On 2 February (Candlemas) a procession ends with blessed navettes.
new.q: Abbaye Saint-Victor, Place Saint-Victor, Marseille

new.title: Stroll under the Palais Longchamp cascade
new.desc: This 1869 monumental fountain by Henri Espérandieu celebrates the arrival of the Canal de Marseille's water. Its wings hold the Fine Arts Museum and the Natural History Museum, and a park lies behind.
new.tip: Park is free; museums open Tuesday to Sunday and are closed on Mondays. Metro 1 to Cinq-Avenues Longchamp.
new.q: Palais Longchamp, Boulevard du Jardin Zoologique, Marseille

new.title: Tour Le Corbusier's Cité Radieuse
new.desc: Completed in 1952, this concrete housing block on pilotis is the prototype of the Unité d'Habitation and part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2016. It has shops, a hotel, the MAMO art centre and a rooftop terrace.
new.tip: Common areas and rooftop are open to visitors at set hours; guided tours (rooftop, shopping street, show flat) need booking via the tourist office.
new.q: Cité Radieuse Le Corbusier, 280 Boulevard Michelet, Marseille

new.title: Sail to the Château d'If of Monte Cristo fame
new.desc: The fortress was built by François I in 1531 on an island in the bay and later served as a state prison. It is the setting of Alexandre Dumas's The Count of Monte Cristo.
new.tip: Boats leave from 1 Quai de la Fraternité (Vieux-Port), about 15 to 20 minutes each way. Entry is ticketed; the château is closed Mondays off-season and mistral winds can stop landings.
new.q: Château d'If, Île d'If, Marseille

new.title: See the Hôpital Caroline quarantine ruins on Frioul
new.desc: Built in the 1820s on Île de Ratonneau as a quarantine hospital (lazaret) for ships, it was partly destroyed by bombing in 1944 and is a listed monument undergoing slow restoration. Its arched ruins face the port of Frioul.
new.tip: Mostly closed to the public; open on special days such as European Heritage Days and for summer concerts. Ferry from the Vieux-Port, then walk from the port.
new.q: Hôpital Caroline, Archipel du Frioul, Marseille

new.title: Admire the fishing hamlet of Vallon des Auffes
new.desc: A tiny fishing port with pointu boats under the Corniche bridge, ringed by seafood restaurants. It is a listed site and still a working harbour with fishermen's cabanons.
new.tip: Visit at sunset; take bus 83 from the Vieux-Port or walk along the Corniche from the Monument aux Morts de l'Armée d'Orient.
new.q: Vallon des Auffes, Rue du Vallon des Auffes, Marseille

new.title: See the Palais du Pharo and its gardens
new.desc: Napoleon III had this palace built from 1858 for his wife Eugénie, overlooking the harbour entrance. The gardens (Jardin Émile-Duclaux) give a view of the Vieux-Port, the MuCEM and the northern coast.
new.tip: Gardens are free (open about 7:00 to 21:00, closed in weather alerts); the palace is mostly reserved for events. Good for a picnic at sunset.
new.q: Palais du Pharo, 58 Boulevard Charles Livon, Marseille

new.title: Visit Château Borély and the Parc Borély
new.desc: An 18th-century neoclassical country house built for Louis Borély, now the Museum of Decorative Arts, Faience and Fashion. It sits in a park of about 17 hectares with pools and a rose garden.
new.tip: Park is free but can close in strong winds, which also shuts the museum; check the museum's closing day on musees.marseille.fr.
new.q: Château Borély, Avenue Clot Bey, Marseille

new.title: See the Orange Vélodrome stadium
new.desc: Home of Olympique de Marseille, this stadium of about 67,000 seats hosted the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2016 and has a distinctive arched roof from its 2014 renovation. Its stands are famous for their atmosphere.
new.tip: Stadium tours (changing rooms, tunnel, press room) run mainly on non-match days and in school holidays; book online. Metro 2 to Rond-Point du Prado.
new.q: Stade Orange Vélodrome, 3 Boulevard Michelet, Marseille

new.title: Walk L'Estaque, the harbour that inspired Cézanne
new.desc: This fishing village in northern Marseille drew Cézanne, Braque, Dufy and Renoir. A marked painters' trail with panels showing reproductions of their canvases loops past the port, pastel houses and viaducts above the bay.
new.tip: Allow about 2 hours for the Chemin des Peintres; the start is on the waterfront opposite Le Littoral restaurant. Free, open daylight hours.
new.q: Port de L'Estaque, Marseille

new.title: Reach the end of the road at Les Goudes
new.desc: A rocky fishing hamlet at the southern end of the Marseille coast, with a small port, cabanons and views of Île Maire. It is a gateway to the Calanques National Park.
new.tip: Metro 2 to Rond-Point du Prado, bus 19 to Madrague de Montredon, then bus 20 to Les Goudes and Callelongue; a seasonal sea shuttle also runs from the Vieux-Port.
new.q: Les Goudes, Marseille

new.title: Step into ancient Massalia at the Jardin des Vestiges
new.desc: Found in 1967 during construction of the Centre Bourse, the remains of the Greek port of Massalia include fortifications possibly from the 6th century BC. A 23 m ship of the 3rd century is displayed in the neighbouring Musée d'Histoire de Marseille.
new.tip: Garden is free; the museum is closed on Mondays. Enter through the museum on the Centre Bourse side.
new.q: Jardin des Vestiges, Centre Bourse, Marseille

new.title: Discover Le Panier's lanes and Place de Lenche
new.desc: Marseille's oldest district is a maze of steep lanes with murals, boutiques and artists' studios. Place de Lenche is said to occupy the site of the Greek agora and is home to the Théâtre de Lenche.
new.tip: Wander uphill from the Hôtel de Ville; weekday mornings are quiet. Bus 49 stops at Place de Lenche.
new.q: Place de Lenche, Le Panier, Marseille

new.title: Hunt street art on the Cours Julien
new.desc: A pedestrian plaza of cafés and shops in the bohemian heart of Marseille, once a fruit-and-vegetable market. Street art took off here with a festival in 2014, and many shopfronts and walls carry commissioned murals.
new.tip: Look for street art around Rue Pastoret and the neighbouring lanes; the tourist office runs guided street-art walks.
new.q: Cours Julien, Marseille

new.title: Taste navettes at Le Four des Navettes
new.desc: Marseille's oldest bakery, dating to 1781, bakes the boat-shaped orange-blossom biscuit navette in the same vaulted oven. The shop stands beside the Saint-Victor abbey, and the Candlemas procession ends here.
new.tip: Open daily around 8:00 to 19:00 (Sunday hours vary); on 2 February expect queues for the blessed navettes.
new.q: Le Four des Navettes, 136 Rue Sainte, Marseille

new.title: Order bouillabaisse at Chez Fonfon
new.desc: A family restaurant that has served bouillabaisse in the Vallon des Auffes since 1952, to a recipe handed down over four generations. The fish soup comes with the fish, rouille and croûtons.
new.tip: Reserve ahead and ask for the bouillabaisse (about 50 euros); opening days vary by season, so check chez-fonfon.com.
new.q: Chez Fonfon, 140 Rue du Vallon des Auffes, Marseille

new.title: Eat bouillabaisse at Le Miramar on the Vieux-Port
new.desc: Founded in 1965 and led by chef Christian Buffa, this harbour-front restaurant is a signatory of the Bouillabaisse Charter. It serves the traditional fish soup with the fish and rouille.
new.tip: Reserve at least 24 hours ahead and order the bouillabaisse when booking.
new.q: Le Miramar, 12 Quai du Port, Marseille

new.title: Dine on bouillabaisse at Chez Michel, Brasserie des Catalans
new.desc: A family seafood restaurant open since 1946 on the Catalans bay, known for bouillabaisse and bourride. Gault&Millau calls it, for many, the best bouillabaisse in Marseille.
new.tip: Book ahead; the bouillabaisse is expensive (roughly 60 to 80 euros) and needs ordering in advance.
new.q: Chez Michel, 6 Rue des Catalans, Marseille

new.title: Taste bouillabaisse at Chez Loury
new.desc: A restaurant (also called Le Mistral) just off the Vieux-Port that makes its bouillabaisse in house, served in three courses. It has a small flower-decked terrace.
new.tip: Reserve and order the bouillabaisse when booking (about 48 euros); open days vary, check loury.com.
new.q: Chez Loury, 3 Rue Fortia, Marseille

new.title: Sip pastis at La Maison du Pastis
new.desc: A shop and tasting room on the Quai du Port dedicated to the anise spirit created in Marseille by Paul Ricard in 1932. It offers dozens of pastis and absinthes and makes its own.
new.tip: Open daily; tastings cost roughly 5 to 10 euros. Pastis is traditionally served with ice-cold water.
new.q: La Maison du Pastis, 108 Quai du Port, Marseille

new.title: Lunch at Les Arcenaulx bookshop-restaurant
new.desc: Housed in the former 17th-century galley arsenal, this restaurant sits beside a bookshop and publisher. Chef Éric Cornilleau cooks classic Provençal dishes among shelves of books and bottles.
new.tip: Closed Sundays; lunch is the better value. Check hours before going.
new.q: Les Arcenaulx, 25 Cours d'Estienne d'Orves, Marseille

new.title: Order a pastis at Le Bar de la Marine
new.desc: Presented as the bar of Marcel Pagnol's Marius trilogy, this café sits at 15 Quai de Rive Neuve on the south side of the Vieux-Port, near the ferry landing. It is also the setting of a scene in the film Love Actually.
new.tip: Open from early morning until late; the terrace is buzzing at weekends.
new.q: Bar de la Marine, 15 Quai de Rive Neuve, Marseille

new.title: Have a drink at La Caravelle with a harbour view
new.desc: A bar-restaurant on the Quai du Port with a small balcony terrace overlooking the harbour and Notre-Dame de la Garde. It is known for jazz and pop concerts, usually on Wednesdays and Fridays.
new.tip: The balcony has only about ten seats, so arrive early for a spot at sunset.
new.q: La Caravelle, 34 Quai du Port, Marseille

new.title: Eat pizza at Chez Étienne in the Panier
new.desc: A Panier institution since 1943 with no long menu: pizza with cheese or anchovy (or half and half) and fried supions are the classics.
new.tip: No reservations, so expect a queue; closed Sundays and cards may not be accepted, so bring cash.
new.q: Chez Étienne, 43 Rue de Lorette, Marseille

new.title: Try aïoli at Chez Madie Les Galinettes
new.desc: A traditional table on the Quai du Port run since 1995 by Delphine Roux, serving Provençal dishes such as aïoli with vegetables and salt cod, plus bouillabaisse at a moderate price.
new.tip: Aïoli is a Friday lunch special at some Marseille restaurants; check the day's menu.
new.q: Chez Madie Les Galinettes, 138 Quai du Port, Marseille

new.title: Dine at L'Épuisette by the sea
new.desc: A Michelin-starred seafood restaurant on the rocks above the Vallon des Auffes, founded in 1953, with views over the harbour and the Frioul islands. Bouillabaisse is its signature dish.
new.tip: Reserve weeks ahead; the kitchen changed hands recently, so check l-epuisette.fr for the current format and open days.
new.q: L'Épuisette, 158 Rue du Vallon des Auffes, Marseille

new.title: Splurge at Le Petit Nice on the Corniche
new.desc: Gérald Passédat's three-Michelin-star restaurant and Relais & Châteaux hotel sits in a villa over the sea at the Anse de Maldormé. Passédat has owned it since 1985 and specialises in Mediterranean fish.
new.tip: Book months ahead; lunch menus are the most accessible.
new.q: Le Petit Nice Passédat, Anse de Maldormé, Corniche Kennedy, Marseille

new.title: Walk down to the Calanque de Sormiou
new.desc: One of the biggest of Marseille's calanques, a fjord-like cove with a pebble beach and fishermen's cabanons set under limestone cliffs.
new.tip: The access road is closed to cars in summer (June to September) without a pass; walk in from the bus stops at La Cayolle or Les Baumettes. Closed to everyone on red fire-risk days. Bring water.
new.q: Calanque de Sormiou, Marseille

new.title: Hike to the Calanque de Morgiou
new.desc: A narrow inlet with a tiny harbour and a handful of fishermen's houses. From Luminy the GR98-51 path reaches it in about 45 minutes, and it continues to Sugiton.
new.tip: Cars are restricted in season and the massif is closed on red fire-risk days; check the park website before the hike.
new.q: Calanque de Morgiou, Marseille

new.title: Reserve a swim at the Calanque de Sugiton
new.desc: One of the most beautiful calanques, reached on foot from the Luminy campus (about 45 minutes, 30 minutes to the viewpoint). On peak summer dates a free reservation is required, with a daily visitor quota.
new.tip: Booking is free on the national park website; in 2026 it applied from 27 June to 30 August plus some weekends in June and September, so check the current dates. Bus B1 to Luminy.
new.q: Calanque de Sugiton, Marseille

new.title: Hike from Callelongue to Marseilleveyre
new.desc: From the end of the bus line at Callelongue a trail climbs toward the summit of Marseilleveyre (433 m), about 600 m of ascent in a roughly 4-hour loop, with sea views and exposed rocky sections.
new.tip: Bus 20 to the Callelongue terminus. Start early, bring water; not for those prone to vertigo, and trails close on red fire-risk days.
new.q: Calanque de Callelongue, Marseille

new.title: Take the boat to the Frioul islands
new.desc: A crossing of about 20 minutes from the Vieux-Port to Ratonneau and Pomègues, with coves for swimming and walking trails; the Frioul If Express boat also serves the Château d'If.
new.tip: Boats leave from Quai de la Fraternité; a return to both islands cost about 16.70 euros. Bring a swimsuit and water.
new.q: Quai de la Fraternité, Vieux-Port, Marseille

new.title: Browse the Marché des Capucins
new.desc: Marseille's multicultural food market in the Noailles district. Stalls sell spices, fruit and vegetables, fish, olives and North African specialities.
new.tip: Open mornings to about 19:00, Tuesday to Saturday (some sources add Monday); closed Sunday. Go early.
new.q: Marché des Capucins, Place des Capucins, Marseille

new.title: Watch the fish market on the Quai de la Fraternité
new.desc: Each morning about ten stalls set up on the Vieux-Port quay opposite the Canebière, where local fishermen or their wives sell the night's catch.
new.tip: Mornings from about 8:00 to 13:00; best before 10:00 when the crowds arrive.
new.q: Marché aux poissons, Quai de la Fraternité, Marseille

new.title: Swim at Plage des Catalans
new.desc: A small sandy beach in the 7th arrondissement, the most central in the city, named after Catalan fishermen. It has a volleyball court, showers and restaurants above the sand.
new.tip: Free; lifeguards on duty in summer. Bus 82 or 83, and avoid the busy afternoon.
new.q: Plage des Catalans, Marseille

new.title: Relax on the Plages du Prado
new.desc: A large seaside park of about 26 hectares reclaimed from the sea with spoil from the metro tunnels, with the David beach, a promenade and a replica of Michelangelo's David. Busy in summer.
new.tip: Lifeguards roughly 9:30 to 19:00 in season. Bus 83 runs along the Corniche from the Vieux-Port.
new.q: Plage du Prado, Avenue Pierre Mendès France, Marseille

new.title: Swim and paddle at Pointe Rouge
new.desc: A sandy beach fronting one of the city's largest marinas, popular with families and watersports (sailing, kayak, paddleboard). Cafés and restaurants line the port.
new.tip: Bus 19 from the Rond-Point du Prado, or the sea shuttle from the Vieux-Port. Check water-quality alerts.
new.q: Plage de la Pointe Rouge, Marseille

new.title: Walk the Corniche Kennedy
new.desc: A coastal promenade of about 4.3 km, easy walking, from the Plage des Catalans past the Vallon des Auffes and the Monument aux Morts de l'Armée d'Orient, with many sea viewpoints.
new.tip: Go at sunset for the light; bus 83 returns to the Vieux-Port.
new.q: Corniche Kennedy, Marseille

new.title: Dance at the Fiesta des Suds festival
new.desc: An annual world-music and electronic festival each October. The 2025 edition (9 to 12 October) was held on the J4 esplanade with a late-night club at the Dock des Suds; the 2026 edition was listed for 8 to 11 October.
new.tip: Check the dates and book tickets in advance; the venue can change between editions.
new.q: Esplanade du J4, Marseille

new.title: Cruise the Calanques by boat
new.desc: Boat trips from the Vieux-Port, operated by Croisières Marseille Calanques and Icard Maritime, sail past the bay islands, Les Goudes, Callelongue and calanques such as Sormiou and Morgiou, some going on to Cassis.
new.tip: Boarding at the corner of Quai des Belges and Quai du Port; routes and durations vary, so check and book in advance in summer.
new.q: Quai des Belges, Vieux-Port, Marseille

new.title: Cross the Vieux-Port on the Ferry Boat
new.desc: A tiny ferry has crossed the harbour since 1880, about 283 m between the Quai du Port (Hôtel de Ville) and the Quai de Rive Neuve facing Place aux Huiles. The crossing takes 3 to 4 minutes.
new.tip: Runs through the day, weather permitting; the fare is nominal.
new.q: Ferry Boat, Quai du Port, Marseille

new.title: Snack on panisses at La Boîte à Panisses
new.desc: Panisse is Marseille's chickpea-flour fry, cooked in crispy sticks. This small restaurant in the old town serves them with French and Mediterranean dishes.
new.tip: Closed Mondays; lunch Tuesday to Sunday, dinner Thursday to Saturday. Check hours before going.
new.q: La Boîte à Panisses, 23 Rue Caisserie, Marseille

new.title: Ride through the Cosquer cave replica
new.desc: The Cosquer Méditerranée replica in the Villa Méditerranée has been open since June 2022. Visitors ride in small modules along a 220 m route in about 35 minutes through a faithful copy of the 33,000-year-old painted cave, whose original entrance lies underwater.
new.tip: Open daily; book on grotte-cosquer.com. Allow about an hour including the exhibition; the entrance is next to the MuCEM.
new.q: Cosquer Méditerranée, Promenade Robert Laffont, Marseille
